```{r setup-theme, echo = F, results = "asis"}
theme_endome <- function(base_size = 11, legend_pos = "top"){
  bs <- base_size

  custom_theme <- theme_gray(base_size = bs) +
    theme(
      plot.title = element_text(size = bs * 1.27, face = "bold", hjust = 0, vjust = 1, margin = margin(b = bs/2)),
      plot.subtitle = element_text(size = bs*0.82),
      panel.border = element_rect(colour = "black", fill = NA, linewidth = 0.5),
      panel.background = element_rect(fill = "#FBFBFB", color = NA),
      axis.text.x = ggplot2::element_text(color = "black", size = bs*0.82, angle = 0, hjust = 0.5),
      axis.text.y = ggplot2::element_text(color = "black", size = bs*0.82),
      axis.title.x = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", size = bs, margin = margin(t = 5)),
      axis.title.y = ggplot2::element_text(face = "bold", size = bs, margin = margin(r = 10)),
      panel.grid.minor = element_blank(),
      panel.grid.major.y = element_line(color = "#444444", linewidth = 0.05, linetype = 2, inherit.blank = TRUE),
      panel.grid.major.x = element_line(color = "#888888", linewidth = 0.05, linetype = 1, inherit.blank = TRUE),
      legend.title = element_text(size = bs * 1.09),
      legend.text = element_text(size = bs * 0.82),
      legend.position = legend_pos,
      legend.key = element_rect(colour = "black", linewidth = 0.01),
      legend.key.size = unit(bs*1.5, "pt"),
      legend.key.spacing.y = unit(bs*0.15, "pt"),
      legend.spacing.y = unit(bs*0.2, "pt"),
      strip.text.x = element_text(color = "black", face = "bold", size = bs*0.82),
      strip.background = element_rect(color = "black", linewidth = 0.5, linetype = "solid"),
      strip.text.y = element_text(color = "black", face = "bold", size = bs*0.82),
      plot.margin = margin(0.5, 0.5, 0.2, 0.5, "cm"),
    )

  if(legend_pos == "top.right"){
    legend_top.right <- theme(
      legend.position = "top",
      legend.justification = "right",
      legend.margin = margin(0, 0, 0, 0), # inside the legend box
      legend.box.margin = margin(-bs*2.2, 0, 0, 0), # around the legend box
      legend.box.spacing = unit(bs*0.5, "pt")
    )
    custom_theme <- custom_theme + legend_top.right
  }else if(legend_pos == "inside.right"){
    legend_inside.right <- theme(
      legend.position = "inside",
      legend.position.inside = c(1, 1),
      legend.justification.inside = c(1, 1),
      legend.background = element_rect(fill = NA, colour = NA),
    )
    custom_theme <- custom_theme + legend_inside.right
  }

  custom_theme
}
```

# Introduction

This report characterizes every *ENDome* built from a single assembled transcriptome to answer how much biological information is lost when the transcripts are collapsed into a single quantification unit (*bin*), and how much that loss changes with different parameters (i.e. ORF filtration, truncation width and truncation end).

To answer these questions, we first account for the merge itself (how the transcripts are distributed in the different bins), then describe the distribution of the per-bin *Bin Information Content* (BIC) score, and lastly identify the features that drive the score and the bins that suffer the most. All information is extracted from the ENDome relational database produced by the pipeline.

## Motivation {-}

The pseudoalignment software employed in the ENDome pipeline (`scUTRquant`, a `kallisto`/`bustools` wrapper) does not quantify transcripts, but rather **bins**. After the transcriptome has been assembled, cleaned and ORF-annotated, the package `txendcutr` truncates every transcript to a fixed length around one of its ends (3' vs 5' truncation). Then, transcripts of the same gene are merged if their ends (the truncation sites) lie less than `merge_distance` apart. What survives after the merge is a bin, a single representative sequence that stands for every transcript that collapsed into it. The kallisto index, the count matrix and the differential-usage test downstream live at that resolution.

Thus, a 3' or 5'-tagged read cannot distinguish between two isoforms whose ends lie within `merge_distance` of each other. A bin whose members encode the same protein, initiate and terminate at the same codons and share the same NMD fate loses nothing when collapsed. However, a bin that merges a protein-coding isoform with a truncated, NMD-sensitive one is a different object entirely. Its abundance can still change between conditions, but it no longer maps onto any single biological event. The two cases are indistinguishable in the count matrix.

The **Bin Information Content** is the score that separates them. Every bin is assigned a number between $[0, 1]$ measuring how much information is preserved when its members are collapsed. In this context, `1` means that the members are functionally interchangeable at the resolution of the features we can measure, and values approaching `0` mean the bin is a mixture. As the metric stands right now, it is computed from the ORF and protein features of the member transcripts, aggregated over every within-bin transcript pair with *Gower's general coefficient* and *Rao's quadratic entropy*. More information regarding these in the [Methods](#methods) section.

## How to read this report {-}

An assembled transcriptome (dataset, sample group and assembly merge method) generates several ENDomes. They share the assembly and the all-vs-all protein search, and differ in three settings: i) the ORF filter (`orf_filter`, which transcripts enter the ENDome), ii) the length of the window kept by the truncation (`width`), and iii) the end that window is anchored to (`txEnd`). ENDomes with different ORF filters start from different transcript sets, so a difference in their bin counts is not only an effect of the truncation. Widths and truncation sites are best compared within the same ORF filter.

The report aims to cover three questions:

1. **How merged are the different transcripts?** What fraction of bins hold each number of transcripts, and what fraction of the transcriptome sits in each class.
2. **How much information survives the merging step?** The distribution of the score, broken down by bin size under different variants, and how it changes between ENDomes.
3. **What drives the loss of information?** Which of the different dissimilarity components contributes most, and which bins are the most affected.

```{r report-settings}
params <- snakemake@params
```

## File paths {-}

The following section defines the input and output paths of the report. The ENDomes are read from the names of the input databases (`<prefix>.<orf_filter>.w<width>.<txEnd>.duckdb`), and ordered by ORF filter, truncation site and width:

```{r script-paths}
# Snakemake inputs
smk_inputs <- snakemake@input
smk_outputs <- snakemake@output
wc <- snakemake@wildcards

## Root of the repository
main_path <- fs::path_abs(fs::path_expand(file.path(snakemake@scriptdir, "..", "..")))
rel_to_main <- \(p, base = main_path) fs::path_rel(fs::path_abs(fs::path_expand(p)), base)

#' ENDome of each DuckDB, read from <prefix>.<orf_filter>.w<width>.<txEnd>.duckdb
#'
#' @param path DuckDB paths
#' @return The paths, named by their ENDome
endomeFromPath <- function(path){
  path <- unlist(path)
  if(length(path) == 0) return(stats::setNames(character(0), character(0)))
  endome <- sub("^.*\\.([^.]+\\.w[^.]+\\.[35]p)\\.duckdb$", "\\1", basename(path))
  unparsed <- endome == basename(path)

  if(any(unparsed)) stop("Cannot read the ENDome from: ", paste(path[unparsed], collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)
  stats::setNames(path.expand(path), endome)
}

#' Label of the width wildcard ("500 bp", "Full length" or as is)
widthLabel <- function(width){
  dplyr::case_when(
    grepl("^[0-9]+$", width) ~ paste0(width, " bp"),
    width == "full" ~ "Full length",
    TRUE ~ width
  )
}

#' Label of an ORF filter preset from filter_labels, or its name if it has none
filterLabel <- function(orf_filter){
  orf_filter <- as.character(orf_filter) # a factor would index by its level codes
  dplyr::coalesce(unname(filter_labels[orf_filter]), orf_filter)
}

## Input databases
duckdb_paths <- endomeFromPath(smk_inputs$duckdb)
if(length(duckdb_paths) == 0) stop("No ENDome DuckDB in the inputs", call. = FALSE)
if(anyDuplicated(names(duckdb_paths))){
  stop("ENDomes given more than once: ",
       paste(unique(names(duckdb_paths)[duplicated(names(duckdb_paths))]), collapse = ", "),
       call. = FALSE)
}
missing_paths <- duckdb_paths[!file.exists(duckdb_paths)]
if(length(missing_paths) > 0) stop("ENDome DuckDB not found: ", paste(missing_paths, collapse = ", "), call. = FALSE)

## ENDomes
endome_parts <- stringr::str_match(names(duckdb_paths), "^([^.]+)\\.w([^.]+)\\.([35]p)$")
endome_info <- tibble::tibble(
  endome = names(duckdb_paths),
  orf_filter = endome_parts[, 2],
  txEnd = endome_parts[, 4],
  width = endome_parts[, 3],
  path = unname(duckdb_paths)
) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    orf_filter = forcats::fct_inorder(orf_filter),
    orf_filter_label = filterLabel(orf_filter),
    width_num = suppressWarnings(as.numeric(width)),
    width_label = widthLabel(width),
    txEnd_label = dplyr::if_else(txEnd == "3p", "3' End", "5' End")
  ) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(orf_filter, txEnd, is.na(width_num), width_num, width) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    label = paste(orf_filter_label, txEnd_label, width_label, sep = " | "), # tables, captions and subtitles
    short_label = paste(txEnd_label, width_label, sep = " | "), # within an ORF filter
    tab_label = paste0(orf_filter_label, "<br>", short_label) # tab headers (HTML)
  )

endomes <- endome_info$endome
duckdb_paths <- duckdb_paths[endomes]
endome_labels <- stats::setNames(endome_info$label, endomes)
tab_labels <- stats::setNames(endome_info$tab_label, endomes)

orf_filters <- levels(endome_info$orf_filter)
filter_tab_labels <- stats::setNames(filterLabel(orf_filters), orf_filters)

## Tab layout, with at most max_tabs_per_row tabs per row
tabClass <- function(per_row){
  n_cols <- ceiling(per_row / ceiling(per_row / max_tabs_per_row))
  paste0(".tabset .", tab_style, min(max(n_cols, 2), 7))
}
tab_class <- tabClass(max(table(endome_info$orf_filter)))
filter_tab_class <- tabClass(length(orf_filters))

## Height of the figures with one row per ENDome
overview_fig_height <- 1.8 + 0.45 * length(endomes) + 0.3 * length(orf_filters)

### Helper library
lib_dir <- path.expand(file.path(snakemake@scriptdir, "../lib"))
if(!dir.exists(lib_dir)) lib_dir <- path.expand(file.path(snakemake@scriptdir, "lib"))
source(file.path(lib_dir, "hf-notebooks.R")) # renderTable()
```

The table below lists the ENDomes of this render and their databases, relative to the main path (`r main_path`). The helper library is read from `r paste0("./", rel_to_main(lib_dir))`.

```{r script-paths-table, echo = FALSE}
endome_info %>%
  dplyr::transmute(ENDome = endome, `ORF filter` = as.character(orf_filter), Label = orf_filter_label,
                   `Truncation site` = txEnd_label, Width = width_label, DuckDB = paste0("./", rel_to_main(path))) %>%
  renderTable(style = "md", caption = sprintf("ENDomes of %s and their databases.", wc$prefix))
```

## Variables and parameters {-}

Two different sets of values (defined in the snakemake pipeline) control what this report describes:

+ The **wildcards** identify the ENDomes. The rule only receives the `prefix` (dataset, sample group and assembly merge method), and the other three are read off the name of each DuckDB file, built as `<prefix>.<orf_filter>.w<width>.<txEnd>.duckdb`.

+ The **parameters** identify the *scoring*, and are the ones `05d-Compute_Scores.R` was invoked with. They describe how the truncation sites were merged into bins (`merge_distance`), which normalization of the `MMseqs2` bit-score defines protein similarity (`protein_metric`), how CDS length differences are mapped onto $[0, 1]$ (`length_scaling`), and how much each member transcript weighs inside its bin (`member_weights`). They are shared by every ENDome of the report.

```{r script-parameters}
# Bin Information parameters, shared by every ENDome
protein_metric <- params$protein_metric
length_scaling <- params$length_scaling
member_weights <- params$member_weights
merge_distance <- params$merge_distance
component_weights <- unlist(params$component_weights)
```

```{r parameter-table, echo = FALSE}
parameter_tbl <- tibble::tribble(
  ~Parameter, ~Value, ~Description,
  "prefix", wc$prefix, "Dataset, sample group and transcript merge method",
  "orf_filter", paste(orf_filters, collapse = "<br>"), "ORF/biotype filtering presets applied before truncation",
  "width", paste(unique(endome_info$width_label), collapse = "<br>"), "Lengths of the retained window at the truncation site",
  "txEnd", paste(unique(endome_info$txEnd_label), collapse = "<br>"), "Truncation sites",
  "merge_distance", as.character(merge_distance), "Max distance (bp) between two truncation sites for them to merge into a single bin",
  "protein_metric", protein_metric, "Which normalization of the MMseqs2 bit score defined protein similarity",
  "length_scaling", length_scaling, "How the CDS length difference is mapped onto [0, 1]",
  "member_weights", member_weights, "Weight given to each member transcript inside a bin"
)

parameter_tbl %>%
  kableExtra::kable(caption = "ENDome wildcards and scoring parameters", format = "html", escape = FALSE) %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "bordered"),
    full_width = TRUE,
    position = "left"
  ) %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "20%") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "20%") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(3, width = "60%") %>%
  kableExtra::row_spec(0:nrow(parameter_tbl), extra_css = "vertical-align: middle;")
```

The `component_weights` set how much each of the five features compared within a bin contributes to the final distance, and are described in [The Dissimilarity Components](#dissimilarity-components). Only their *ratios* matter, since Gower renormalizes by the total comparable weight, which is what the `Relative Contribution` column reports:

```{r weight-table, echo = FALSE}
tibble::enframe(component_weights, name = "Component", value = "Weight") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    `Relative Contribution` = Weight / sum(Weight),
    Description = dplyr::recode(Component,
      protein = "1 - bit-score ratio of the two ORF proteins (MMseqs2)",
      cds_len = "Relative difference in CDS length",
      start_codon = "Graded disagreement of the initiation codon",
      stop_codon = "Graded disagreement of the termination codon",
      nmd = "Disagreement of the predicted NMD fate",
      .default = "-")
  ) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(dplyr::desc(Weight)) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(`Relative Contribution` = scales::percent(`Relative Contribution`, accuracy = 0.1)) %>%
  kableExtra::kable(caption = "ENDome component weights in use.") %>%
  kableExtra::kable_styling(
    bootstrap_options = c("striped", "hover", "condensed", "bordered"),
    full_width = TRUE,
    position = "left"
  )
```

There are also local helpers used in this report:

```{r helper-functions}
# Formatting
fmtInt <- function(x) format(round(x), big.mark = ",", trim = TRUE, scientific = FALSE)
fmtNum <- function(x, digits = 3) formatC(x, format = "f", digits = digits)
fmtPct <- function(x, accuracy = 0.1) scales::percent(x, accuracy = accuracy)

# Scores
## Centre of the histogram bin of each score (a score of 1 goes to the last bin)
scoreBinCentre <- function(x, binwidth) (pmin(floor(x / binwidth), ceiling(1 / binwidth) - 1) + 0.5) * binwidth

scoreBand <- function(x){
  cut(x, breaks = c(-Inf, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9, 1 - 1e-9, Inf),
      labels = c("< 0.5", "0.5 - 0.7", "0.7 - 0.9", "0.9 - 1", "= 1"),
      right = FALSE, ordered_result = TRUE)
}

#' Labels of the size classes, e.g. c(1, 2, 5, 10) gives "1", "2", "3-5", "6-10" and "11+"
sizeLabels <- function(breaks){
  lower <- c(1, utils::head(breaks, -1) + 1)
  c(dplyr::if_else(lower == breaks, as.character(breaks), paste0(lower, "-", breaks)),
    paste0(max(breaks) + 1, "+"))
}

#' Bucket a count (bin members, bins per gene...) into an ordered factor
#'
#' @param n Counts
#' @param breaks Upper bounds of the classes
#' @param labels One label per class plus the open tail. Defaults to sizeLabels(breaks)
#' @param drop Whether to drop the empty classes
sizeClass <- function(n, breaks = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 10, 20), labels = NULL, drop = FALSE){
  if(is.null(labels)) labels <- sizeLabels(breaks)
  out <- cut(n, breaks = c(0, breaks, Inf), labels = labels, right = TRUE, ordered_result = TRUE)
  if(drop) out <- droplevels(out)
  out
}

#' The three score variants of a per-bin table in long format
pivotScores <- function(df){
  df %>%
    dplyr::select(endome, bin_id, n_members, size_class, dplyr::all_of(names(score_levels))) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::all_of(names(score_levels)), names_to = "score", values_to = "value") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(score = factor(score_levels[score], levels = unname(score_levels)))
}

#' Summary of the value column by the groups in ...
summariseScores <- function(df, ...){
  df %>%
    dplyr::group_by(...) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      n_bins = dplyr::n(),
      mean = mean(value, na.rm = TRUE),
      sd = stats::sd(value, na.rm = TRUE),
      min = min(value, na.rm = TRUE),
      q05 = unname(stats::quantile(value, 0.05, na.rm = TRUE)),
      q25 = unname(stats::quantile(value, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)),
      median = stats::median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
      q75 = unname(stats::quantile(value, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)),
      q95 = unname(stats::quantile(value, 0.95, na.rm = TRUE)),
      max = max(value, na.rm = TRUE),
      pct_perfect = mean(value >= 1 - 1e-9, na.rm = TRUE),
      pct_below_09 = mean(value < 0.9, na.rm = TRUE),
      pct_below_07 = mean(value < 0.7, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    )
}

# ENDomes
#' The endome column as a factor in the order of the report
asEndome <- function(df) dplyr::mutate(df, endome = factor(endome, levels = endomes))

#' Rows of one ENDome
forEndome <- function(df, e) dplyr::filter(df, .data$endome == .env$e)

#' Subtitle with the ENDome, its bins and its binned transcripts
endomeSubtitle <- function(e){
  b <- forEndome(bin_summary, e)
  sprintf("%s | %s bins over %s binned transcripts | merge distance %s bp",
          endome_labels[[e]], fmtInt(b$n_bins), fmtInt(b$n_members), merge_distance)
}

# Tabsets
#' Write one tab per key
#'
#' tabsetFun(key) returns a ggplot, a table (kable or DT) or NULL, and can also cat() text.
#' Errors are printed in the tab instead of stopping the report.
#'
#' @param keys ENDomes or ORF filters
#' @param labels Tab headers (HTML), named by key
#' @param tabsetFun Function of one key
#' @param level Header level of the tabs, one more than the header of the tabset
renderTabset <- function(keys, labels, tabsetFun, level = 3){
  invisible(
    lapply(keys, function(k){
      cat("\n\n", strrep("#", level), " ", labels[[k]], " {.unlisted .unnumbered}\n\n", sep = "")

      tryCatch({
        output <- tabsetFun(k)
        if(inherits(output, c("ggplot", "knitr_kable", "kableExtra"))){
          print(output)
        }else if(inherits(output, c("htmlwidget", "shiny.tag", "shiny.tag.list"))){
          ## knit_print registers the JS/CSS dependencies of widgets like DT
          kp <- knitr::knit_print(output)
          knitr::knit_meta_add(attr(kp, "knit_meta"))
          cat(kp)
        }else if(!is.null(output)){
          print(output)
        }
      }, error = function(err) cat("*Not available for ", k, ": ", conditionMessage(err), "*\n\n", sep = ""))
      cat("\n\n")
    })
  )
}

renderTabsetByEndome <- function(tabsetFun, level = 3) renderTabset(endomes, tab_labels, tabsetFun, level)
renderTabsetByFilter <- function(tabsetFun, level = 3) renderTabset(orf_filters, filter_tab_labels, tabsetFun, level)

#' Block that starts collapsed and opens with a button (collapse-toggle of the theme)
#'
#' Use inside a tab of a results = "asis" chunk.
#'
#' @param label Text of the button
#' @param expr Code that prints the content of the block
renderExpandable <- function(label, expr){
  cat("\n\n<button class=\"collapse-toggle\" data-target=\"next\">▶ ", label, "</button>\n\n::: {.tabset-wrapper}\n\n", sep = "")
  force(expr)
  cat("\n\n:::\n\n")
}
```

## Data loading {-}

All data used in this report is read from the DuckDB files of the ENDomes, generated by the pipeline. 

```{r load-data}
## In-memory DuckDB with the database of every ENDome attached read-only
con <- DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb())
db_alias <- stats::setNames(sprintf("endome_%02d", seq_along(endomes)), endomes)
for(e in endomes){
  DBI::dbExecute(con, sprintf("ATTACH %s AS %s (READ_ONLY)", DBI::dbQuoteString(con, duckdb_paths[[e]]), db_alias[[e]]))
}

## Tables of every database
db_tables <- DBI::dbGetQuery(con, "SELECT database_name, table_name, column_count FROM duckdb_tables() WHERE schema_name = 'main'") %>%
  dplyr::filter(database_name %in% db_alias) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(endome = names(db_alias)[match(database_name, db_alias)])

unscored <- setdiff(endomes, db_tables$endome[db_tables$table_name == "bin_information"])
if(length(unscored) > 0){
  stop("`bin_information` is absent from the database of ", paste(unscored, collapse = ", "),
       ". Has S05d-Compute_Scores.R been run on it?", call. = FALSE)
}

## One view per table shared by every database, with the ENDome as first column
shared_tables <- Reduce(intersect, split(db_tables$table_name, db_tables$endome))
for(t in shared_tables){
  sql <- paste(sprintf("SELECT %s AS endome, * FROM %s.main.%s",
                       DBI::dbQuoteString(con, endomes), db_alias[endomes], DBI::dbQuoteIdentifier(con, t)),
               collapse = "\nUNION ALL BY NAME\n")
  DBI::dbExecute(con, sprintf("CREATE TEMP VIEW %s AS %s", DBI::dbQuoteIdentifier(con, t), sql))
}
db <- stats::setNames(lapply(shared_tables, \(t) dplyr::tbl(con, t)), shared_tables)

# Per-bin scores, with the gene and the superseded transcripts of each bin
bin_information <- db$bin_information %>%
  dplyr::select(endome, bin_id, n_members, dplyr::all_of(names(score_levels)),
                n_pairs, n_pairs_scored, q_rao, q_rao_norm, pair_mass,
                dplyr::starts_with("mean_d_")) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(dplyr::select(db$bins, endome, bin_id, gene_id, n_superseded), by = c("endome", "bin_id")) %>%
  dplyr::collect() %>%
  asEndome() %>%
  dplyr::mutate(size_class = sizeClass(n_members), .after = n_members)

# Summaries computed in DuckDB
## Transcripts, the same for every ENDome of an ORF filter
tx_summary <- db$transcripts %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_transcripts = dplyr::n(),
    n_genes = dplyr::n_distinct(gene_id),
    n_superseded = sum(as.integer(!is.na(superseded_by)), na.rm = TRUE),
    n_with_orf = sum(as.integer(!is.na(aa_id)), na.rm = TRUE),
    n_nmd = sum(as.integer(NMD_sensitive), na.rm = TRUE),
    n_unbinned = sum(as.integer(is.na(bin_id)), na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::collect() %>%
  asEndome()

## Bins
bin_summary <- db$bins %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_bins = dplyr::n(),
    n_singleton = sum(as.integer(n_members == 1), na.rm = TRUE),
    n_multi = sum(as.integer(n_members >= 2), na.rm = TRUE),
    n_members = sum(n_members, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::collect() %>%
  asEndome()

## Transcripts by reference isoform status and pigeon category
ref_isoform_counts <- db$transcripts %>%
  dplyr::count(endome, ref_isoform, structural_category, subcategory) %>%
  dplyr::collect() %>%
  asEndome()

## Gene names of the merged bins (a bin can have several) and of every gene
bin_gene_names <- db$transcripts %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(bin_id)) %>%
  dplyr::semi_join(dplyr::filter(db$bins, n_members >= 2), by = c("endome", "bin_id")) %>%
  dplyr::distinct(endome, bin_id, gene_name) %>%
  dplyr::collect() %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome, bin_id) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(gene_name = paste(unique(stats::na.omit(gene_name)), collapse = ", "), .groups = "drop") %>%
  asEndome()

gene_names <- db$transcripts %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(gene_name)) %>%
  dplyr::distinct(gene_id, gene_name) %>%
  dplyr::collect() %>%
  dplyr::distinct(gene_id, .keep_all = TRUE)

# Structure of the databases
## Rows of every table in every database
db_rows <- db_tables %>%
  dplyr::filter(table_name %in% shared_tables) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(sql = sprintf("SELECT %s AS endome, %s AS table_name, count(*) AS n_rows FROM %s.main.%s",
                              DBI::dbQuoteString(con, endome), DBI::dbQuoteString(con, table_name),
                              database_name, DBI::dbQuoteIdentifier(con, table_name))) %>%
  dplyr::pull(sql) %>%
  paste(collapse = "\nUNION ALL\n") %>%
  DBI::dbGetQuery(con, .)

## Keys of the first database, as every database has the same structure
constraintsQuery <- function(type, columns){
  sprintf("SELECT %s FROM duckdb_constraints() WHERE constraint_type = '%s' AND schema_name = 'main' AND database_name = %s",
          columns, type, DBI::dbQuoteString(con, db_alias[[1]]))
}
fk_cols <- "table_name AS child_table, array_to_string(constraint_column_names, ', ') AS child_fk_cols,
            referenced_table AS parent_table, array_to_string(referenced_column_names, ', ') AS parent_key_cols"
pk_cols <- "table_name AS child_table, array_to_string(constraint_column_names, ', ') AS child_pk"

db_keys <- dplyr::left_join(
  DBI::dbGetQuery(con, constraintsQuery("FOREIGN KEY", fk_cols)),
  DBI::dbGetQuery(con, constraintsQuery("PRIMARY KEY", pk_cols)),
  by = "child_table"
) %>%
  dplyr::select(child_table, child_pk, child_fk_cols, parent_table, parent_key_cols) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(child_table, child_fk_cols)

DBI::dbDisconnect(con, shutdown = TRUE)
```

```{r derived-data}
## Merged bins (two or more members), used in every score summary
merged_bins <- bin_information %>%
  dplyr::filter(n_members >= 2) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(size_class = droplevels(size_class))

## The three score variants in long format
scores_long <- pivotScores(bin_information)
merged_long <- pivotScores(merged_bins)

## Bins per gene
gene_bins_df <- bin_information %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(gene_id)) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome, gene_id) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_bins = dplyr::n(),
    n_transcripts = sum(n_members),
    largest_bin = max(n_members),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

### The Database Structure {-}

Every database has the same tables:

+ `transcripts`: one row per transcript of the ORF-filtered transcriptome.
+ `bins`: one row per bin of the ENDome.
+ `bin_information`: one row per bin, with its information content scores.
+ `proteins`: one row per distinct ORF protein sequence.
+ `cds`: one row per distinct CDS locus, with its start/stop codons.
+ `utr5`: one row per distinct 5' UTR locus.
+ `utr3`: one row per distinct 3' UTR locus.

The table below counts their rows in each ENDome, grouped by ORF filter as in the [ENDome numbers](#endome-numbers).. The header of each table gives its number of columns.

```{r db-contents, echo = FALSE}
## Tables in the order of the list above, then any other table
table_order <- c("transcripts", "bins", "bin_information", "proteins", "cds", "utr5", "utr3")
table_order <- c(intersect(table_order, shared_tables), sort(setdiff(shared_tables, table_order)))
table_n_cols <- db_tables %>%
  dplyr::group_by(table_name) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(n_cols = max(column_count), .groups = "drop") %>%
  tibble::deframe()

db_rows %>%
  tidyr::pivot_wider(names_from = table_name, values_from = n_rows) %>%
  asEndome() %>%
  dplyr::left_join(asEndome(dplyr::select(endome_info, endome, orf_filter_label, txEnd_label, width_label)),
                   by = "endome") %>%
  dplyr::arrange(endome) %>%
  dplyr::select(`ORF filter` = orf_filter_label, Site = txEnd_label, Width = width_label, dplyr::all_of(table_order)) %>%
  dplyr::rename_with(\(x) sprintf("%s<br>(%s cols)", x, table_n_cols[x]), dplyr::all_of(table_order)) %>%
  renderTable(style = "md", escape = FALSE, align = c("l", "l", "l", rep("r", length(table_order))),
              caption = "Rows of the tables of every ENDome database.") %>%
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 3, "Rows per table" = length(table_order))) %>%
  kableExtra::collapse_rows(columns = 1, valign = "top")
```

Each table is related to others through primary and foreign keys, declared at write time by `writeDuckTable()`. The following table reads that structure back from DuckDB's own `duckdb_constraints()` catalogue.

```{r db-keys, echo = FALSE}
db_keys %>%
  renderTable(style = "md", caption = "Referential structure of the databases, read from duckdb_constraints().")
```

The surrogate keys (`aa_id`, `cds_id`, `utr5_id`, `utr3_id`) are **content hashes** built from DNA/AA sequences and locus coordinates.

# Methods {.spacer #methods}

<button class="collapse-toggle" data-target="next">▶ Expand to see information about the input data</button>

::: {#collapsible_id .tabset-wrapper}
## Input data {.unlisted .unnumbered }

Bin information content is the last stage of the ENDome pipeline before differential transcript usage identification. Current pipeline looks like this:

| Step | Rule / script | Software | Outputs |
|---|---|---|---|
| 01 | `minimap2_align` | minimap2 | Spliced alignment of the long reads |
| 02 | `stringtie_*` / `isomatch_*` | StringTie, isomatch, gffcompare | Assembled and merged transcript models |
| 03 | `pigeon_*` | pigeon (SQANTI3 lineage) | Structural classification and artifact removal |
| 04 | `ORF_annotate` | ORFannotate | ORF calling: protein, CDS, 5'/3' UTR sequences, NMD prediction |
| 04 | `ORF_categorization` / `ORF_filtration` | `04a`/`04b` (R) | Isoform summary and the `orf_filter` process |
| 05a | `txendcutr_truncation` | `txendcutr` (fork of `txcutr`) | Truncation to the window, **bin definition**, merge and overlap tables |
| 05b | `endome_export_proteins` | `SS05b` (R) | Protein FASTA keyed by content hash, plus the protein map |
| 05 | `endome_mmseqs_search` | MMseqs2 | All-vs-all protein alignment |
| 05c | `endome_build_db` | `S05c` (R) | The ENDome DuckDB |
| 05d | `endome_compute_scores` | `S05d` (R) | Pairwise distances, Gower, Rao, `bin_information` |
| 05 | `endome_info_report` | this document | Characterization of every ENDome of a transcriptome |

Every transcript carries the pigeon (SQANTI3 lineage) `structural_category` and `subcategory` of the isoform summary, and a reference isoform flag (`ref_isoform`) derived from them. A transcript is a reference isoform when pigeon classifies it as a *full-splice match* (FSM), i.e. its intron chain is identical to that of a reference (GENCODE) transcript. Its ends may differ, so FSM transcripts with an alternative 5' or 3' end are reference isoforms too, and `subcategory` tells them apart (`reference_match`, `alternative_5end`, `alternative_3end`, `alternative_3end5end`, `mono-exon`). Every other category is not a reference isoform, whether it is a fragment of a reference transcript (ISM), a new combination of known (NIC) or new (NNC) splice sites, or a transcript outside the annotated splicing (antisense, fusion, genic, intergenic).

<!-- The scoring itself can be summarized in the following steps: -->

<!-- 1. **Transcript membership definition**: read the `bin_id` from `transcripts` and return the bin to transcript mapping. Each member of a bin of size $n$ receives a weight $w_i = 1/n$. -->
<!-- 2. **Feature selection**: every member transcript is joined to its CDS, UTRs, protein content and additional transcript information from `ORFannotate`. -->
<!-- 3. **Transcript pairing**: the within-bin pairs are enumerated and each pair receives one dissimilarity per feature. -->
<!-- 4. **Dissimilarity Combination**: each pair's component dissimilarities are combined into a single Gower distance $d_{ij}$. These distances are symmetric ($d_{ij}=d_{ji}$). -->
<!-- 5. **Aggregation**: the pair distances of each bin are aggregated into Rao's quadratic entropy, and turned into a score stored in the `bin_information` table. -->
:::

## The Dissimilarity components {.tabset .break3 #dissimilarity-components}

The main idea behind the bin information score is to quantify *how different* are the transcripts merged into the same bin. Five features are compared, each yielding a number between $[0, 1]$, where `0` means identical and `1` means maximally different. If a comparison cannot be made, value is represented by `NA`.

### Protein similarity {-}

This component carries the most relevant question about transcript similarity: `do these two transcripts encode the same protein? If not, how different are these proteins?` The weight assigned to this component is `r fmtNum(component_weights[["protein"]], 1)`.

The proteins of the complete ORF-filtered transcriptome are searched **all against all** with *MMseqs2*. MMseqs2 (*Many-against-Many sequence searching*) is a suite designed precisely to search and cluster huge protein and nucleotide sequence sets. Its authors report it running up to 10,000 times faster than BLAST, achieving almost the same sensitivity at 100 times its speed. Given that our protein set is on the order of $10^5$ sequences, MMseqs2 completes the search in minutes.

The **bit score** is preferred over the *percentage identity* (PID) computed with `pwalign::pairwiseAlignment()` mainly because PID ignores the length of the longer protein. It is computed over the aligned region only, so a truncated ORF aligning perfectly inside its full-length parent reaches 100% identity. The bit score grows with the length of the alignment, so once normalized against the self bit score it becomes a measure of *how much of the protein is shared*. The same objection applies to MMseqs2's own `fident` field, which is available but not recommended.

`MMseqs2` works in three stages: i) a $k$-mer prefilter that requires two consecutive similar $k$-mers on the same diagonal, ii) an ungapped diagonal scoring pass, and iii) a vectorised Smith-Waterman alignment of what survives. The settings used here are deliberately permissive because we aim to answer *how similar are the two sequences*:

```{r mmseqs-flag-table, echo = FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Flag, ~Value, ~`What it does`,
  "<code>-s</code>", "7.5", "Prefilter sensitivity. Higher values find more distant homologues, at the cost of speed.",
  "<code>-e</code>", "10000", "E-value cutoff to report a hit. Set high to keep weak alignments.",
  "<code>--add-self-matches</code>", "1", "Aligns every protein to itself.",
  "<code>--alignment-mode</code>", "3", "Reports the score, start and end positions, coverage and identity of every alignment.",
  "<code>-a</code>", "1", "Keeps the alignment backtrace.",
  "<code>--min-ungapped-score</code>", "0", "Minimum score in the ungapped stage for a pair to be aligned. 0 lets every pair through.",
  "<code>-c</code> / <code>--cov-mode</code>", "0 / 0", "Minimum fraction of both sequences covered by the alignment. 0 keeps partial alignments.",
  "<code>--max-seqs</code>", "5000", "Maximum number of targets per query that pass the prefilter. Set high so large paralogue families are not cut.",
  "<code>--max-accept</code> / <code>--max-rejected</code>", "100000", "Number of accepted / rejected alignments after which a query stops being aligned."
) %>%
  renderTable(caption = "MMseqs2 search settings used for the all-vs-all protein search.",
              style = "md", escape = FALSE, row_padding = "3px") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "20%") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "10%") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(3, width = "70%") %>%
  kableExtra::row_spec(0:9, extra_css = "vertical-align: middle;")
```

Raw bit scores are not directly comparable across pairs, as they scale with sequence length. Thus, they are normalized into a *bit-score ratio*, defined in one of these three flavors, where $b_{ij}$ is the bit-score reported by MMseqs2:

$$
\text{BSR}_{\max}(i,j) = \min\left(1, \frac{b_{ij}}{\max(b_{ii}, b_{jj})}\right),
\qquad
\text{BSR}_{\min}(i,j) = \min\left(1, \frac{b_{ij}}{\min(b_{ii}, b_{jj})}\right),
\qquad
\text{BSR}_{\text{mixed}}(i,j) = \min\left(1, \frac{b_{ij}}{\sqrt{b_{ii} b_{jj}}}\right)
$$

The choice between them (`protein_metric`, here **`r protein_metric`**) reflects how we treat containment. A short ORF that aligns perfectly inside a long ORF scores $\approx 1$ under `bsr_min` (permissive approach) and $\approx$ the length ratio under `bsr_max` (conservative approach). The metric `bsr_mixed` is the geometric mean of the two. The final protein distance is defined as $d_{\text{protein}} = 1 - \text{BSR}$.

Two implementation details that matter for these results:

+ Reciprocal hits: MMseqs2 reports both $i \to j$ and $j \to i$ separately, and the two rows can disagree. The row with the highest `bits` is kept.
+ A protein that was never searched makes every pair it belongs to *non-comparable*. That is, the distance is set as `NA` and the component drops out of the Gower weighting. A protein that was searched but returned no hit against another protein is set as completely dissimilar and gets $\text{BSR} = 0$. 

### CDS length {-}

Defined as:

$$
d_{\text{cds_len}} =
\begin{cases}
\dfrac{|L_i - L_j|}{\max(L_i, L_j, 1)} & \text{`ratio`} \\[2ex]
\dfrac{|L_i - L_j|}{\max(L_i + L_j, 1)} & \text{`canberra`}
\end{cases}
$$

with `length_scaling` = **`r length_scaling`**. Both map a ratio variable into $[0, 1]$, with `ratio` being the fraction of the longer CDS that is not shared and `canberra`, which divides by the *sum* of the two lengths instead of the larger one. Since $\max(L_i, L_j) \leq L_i + L_j \leq 2\max(L_i, L_j)$, `canberra` always lies between one half and the whole of `ratio`: it produces the same ordering, but compresses the scale and only approaches 1 in the limit where one of the two lengths goes to zero. In practice it is simply gentler on large differences, as a 1000 nt CDS against a 500 nt one scores 0.50 under `ratio` and 0.33 under `canberra`, while 1000 nt against 100 nt scores 0.90 and 0.82 respectively.

This component is redundant with `d_protein` under `bsr_max`, which is why it carries such a low weight (`r fmtNum(component_weights[["cds_len"]], 2)`). It is kept to separate two ORFs that *align* well but differ in extent.

### Initiation and termination codons {-}

This component is split into three different levels:

```{r codon-distance-table, echo = FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Situation, ~Distance,
  "Same codon", "0",
  "Both canonical, or both non-canonical, but a different codon (e.g. <code>TGA</code> vs <code>TAA</code>)", "0.5",
  "One canonical, the other not", "1"
) %>%
  renderTable(caption = "Distance levels for the initiation and termination codon components.",
              style = "md", escape = FALSE, row_padding = "3px") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, width = "80%") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, bold = TRUE, width = "20%") %>%
  kableExtra::row_spec(0:3, extra_css = "vertical-align: middle;")
```

Canonical means `ATG` for initiation and `TAA`/`TAG`/`TGA` for termination. If the transcript has no ORF (and thus no codon), the component drops out. Given that almost every protein-coding transcript starts at `ATG` and ends at a canonical stop, the vast majority of pairs sit at 0 on both components, and they are only relevant when a bin mixes a canonical ORF with a non-canonical one. They are therefore given a deliberately small weight: start_codon = `r fmtNum(component_weights[["start_codon"]], 2)` and stop_codon = `r fmtNum(component_weights[["stop_codon"]], 2)`.

### NMD Sensitivity {-}

A binary discordance on the `NMD_sensitive` flag reported by `ORFannotate`. It is the second-heaviest component (`r fmtNum(component_weights[["nmd"]], 2)`) because a bin that mixes a stable isoform with an NMD target is collapsing two very different outcomes.

### Others {-}

Several other components were considered and are already implemented in `S05d-Compute_Scores.R`, but are left out of the current score. All of them reuse the same primitives, so enabling one is a matter of adding its column and its weight:

```{r discarded-components-table, echo = FALSE}
tibble::tribble(
  ~Candidate, ~Definition, ~`Why it was left out`,
  "<code>d_junctions</code>", "<code>relativeDelta()</code> of the number of splice junctions", "Largely redundant with the CDS length and the protein components, and it counts junctions anywhere in the transcript, including outside the truncation window",

  "<code>d_utr_binned</code>", "<code>relativeDelta()</code> of the length of the UTR at the truncation site", "It measures the part of the transcript the assay actually reads (the 3' UTR in a 3p ENDome, the 5' UTR in a 5p one), so two members with very different UTR lengths at that end are genuinely different regulatory objects even with identical ORFs",

  "<code>d_structural_cat</code> / <code>d_subcategory</code>", "<code>discordance()</code> of the SQANTI3 structural category and subcategory", "Descriptive of the <em>annotation status</em> of a transcript rather than of its product; two members can differ here while encoding the same protein",

  "<code>d_biotype</code>", "<code>discordance()</code> of <code>ref_gene_type</code> and <code>ref_transcript_type</code>", "Nearly constant under an <code>orf_filter</code> that already selects protein-coding transcripts"
) %>%
  renderTable(caption = "Dissimilarity components implemented but not used in the current score.",
              style = "md", escape = FALSE, row_padding = "3px") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "20%") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(2, width = "30%") %>%
  kableExtra::column_spec(3, width = "50%") %>%
  kableExtra::row_spec(0:4, extra_css = "vertical-align: middle;")
```

Additionally, **domain-level protein similarity** (Pfam/InterPro annotation, which would say *which* part of a protein is shared rather than how much) is also being considered for future iterations of the pipeline.

## Gower's General Coefficient

The dissimilarity components generated in the previous section are of incompatible types. `d_protein` is a continuous, normalized alignment score; `d_cds_len` is a continuous ratio; `d_start_codon` and `d_stop_codon` are three-level ordinal comparisons taking values in $\{0, 0.5, 1\}$; and `d_nmd` is a plain binary discordance. There is no common measurement scale that all five naturally live on, so each has to be mapped into $[0, 1]$ by its own rule.

On top of that, they can produce incomplete comparisons (i.e. a transcript without ORF has no CDS and cannot compare `d_protein` or `d_cds_len`). A standard Euclidean or Manhattan distance is not properly defined in this scenario. For this purpose, Gower's general coefficient of similarity is the right tool. Each variable $k$ is reduced to a per-pair score $d_{ijk} \in [0, 1]$ and a comparability indicator $\delta_{ijk} \in \{0, 1\}$, with the variables combined as a weighted mean over the comparable ones:

$$
d_{ij} = \frac{\sum_k w_k \, \delta_{ijk} \, d_{ijk}}{\sum_k w_k \, \delta_{ijk}}
$$


Two properties make this the right choice here:

1. **Missingness is handled by construction**: a non-comparable variable is removed from both the numerator and denominator, so a pair scored on three variables is neither penalized nor rewarded relative to a pair scored on five. A pair with no comparable variables at all returns `NA` rather than an artificial 0 or 1.
2. **Weights are relative**: because the denominator is the total comparable weight, only the ratios between weights matter. The configured ratios (e.g. protein = `r fmtNum(component_weights[["protein"]], 2)` against NMD = `r fmtNum(component_weights[["nmd"]], 2)`) state how relevant each component is relative to the others. Setting a weight to 0 removes the variable.

### Symmetric and Asymmetric variables {-}

Gower's original formulation distinguishes **symmetric** from **asymmetric** binary variables. For an asymmetric variable, a joint absence (both members sitting in the reference state) carries no information and should be excluded from the comparison ($\delta_{ijk} = 0$). 

Two of our components have this behavior:

- **Codons**: the overwhelming majority of ORFs initiate at `ATG` and terminate at one of the three canonical stops. Two canonical start codons are the null state of the transcriptome, and treating it as evidence of similarity inflates every score.
- **NMD**: most transcripts are not NMD-sensitive. Two NMD-insensitive members agreeing adds no information at all, while two NMD-sensitive members is more informative.

The pipeline therefore emits a second distance, $d_{ij}^{\text{asym}}$, identical to the first except that `d_start_codon`, `d_stop_codon` and `d_nmd` are set to `NA` when both members sit in the reference state. Asymmetric scores are systematically lower and more discriminating for the genuinely mixed bins, at the cost of resting on fewer variables and returning `NA` for a pair on which nothing remains comparable. Both are reported in [Information Content](#information-content) and the choice between them is a reporting decision.

## Rao's quadratic entropy {.tabset .break3}

Since bins are sets and not individual pairs, the pairwise distances must be aggregated. For this purpose, **Rao's quadratic entropy** is the natural aggregate, an originally ecological measure of functional diversity that combines relative abundances with pairwise dissimilarities:

$$
Q = \sum_{i} \sum_{j} p_i \, p_j \, d_{ij}
$$

We can reinterpret its original context with bins being the communities, transcripts being the species and $p_i$ is the relative weight of each member $i$. With `member_weights = "uniform"`, $p_i = 1/n$ for every member of a bin of size $n$. Using this metric allows for the future implementation of weighting members by their expression (not possible at this stage) or any other factor, such as TSL or structural category.

In our current approach, $d_{ij} = d_{ji}$ and $d_{ii} = 0$, so the double sum reduces to the upper triangle:

$$
Q = 2 \sum_{i < j} p_i \, p_j \, d_{ij}
$$

### Normalized score {-}

As it stands, $Q$ depends on the size of the bin by construction. For example, take a bin of $n$ members in which every pair happens to be *equally* dissimilar, then $Q = (1 - 1/n)\,\bar{d}$, the $n$ zero-distance self-comparisons of the diagonal are part of the total mass, and they dilute $Q$ by a factor $1 - 1/n$. The maximum attainable $Q$ therefore grows with bin size (0 for a singleton, 0.5 for a pair, 0.9 for a bin of ten), and a 2-member bin cannot score below 0.5 no matter how unrelated its members are.

That makes it the right quantity for ranking merges by total information lost, but not the most suitable to answer whether the members of a given bin resemble each other. To remove the size term exactly, we define the *comparable pair mass* $M$ as the sum of the pair weights alone, and divide by it:

$$
M = 2 \sum_{i<j} p_i \, p_j \, \delta_{ij}, \qquad
Q_{\texttt{norm}} = \frac{Q}{M}, \qquad
\texttt{info_score_norm} = 1 - Q_{\texttt{norm}}
$$

In this case, $\delta_{ij}$ is 1 when the pair has at least one comparable variable, so $M = 1 - 1/n$ when every pair could be scored. $Q_{\texttt{norm}}$ is then simply the mean pairwise Gower distance over the comparable pairs, and $1 - Q_{\texttt{norm}}$ is directly comparable across bins of any size. This is the default score and the one to use to answer if transcripts within a bin are more heterogeneous than in this other bin.

The two are related by the following identity:

$$
\texttt{info_score} = 1 - (1 - \texttt{info_score_norm}) \cdot M
$$

### Non-normalized score (default Rao's) {-}

The default Rao's metric $Q$ is kept for comparisons, as it answers what is the expected dissimilarity between two individuals drawn at random from the community. Under this assumption, it makes sense that a bin with two completely different transcripts still reports $Q = 0.5$, as there is a 50% chance of drawing the same transcript twice.

$$
\texttt{info_score} = 1 - Q
$$

### Asymmetric approach {-}

Identical to `info_score_norm` but computed from $d_{ij}^{\text{asym}}$, with the reference-state exclusion described above. It is normalized by its own comparable pair mass $M^{\texttt{asym}}$, which is smaller than $M$ whenever a pair lost a component to the reference-state rule.

$$
\texttt{info_score_norm}^{\texttt{asym}} = 1 - Q_{\texttt{norm}}^{\texttt{asym}}
$$

## Singletons

A bin of one transcript has no pairs, and thus $Q = 0$, $M = 0$ and all three scores fall back to 1. These bins are excluded from every distributional summary in this report (except the `All bins` rows of the global summary), as they are usually the majority of the bins.

## Software

The score depends on the following external software and published methods:

```{r software-table, echo = FALSE}
tibble::tribble(

  "txendcutr", "Truncation of the transcriptome to a fixed window and definition of the bins", "Fork of txcutr (Fansler et al.)",
  "MMseqs2", "All-vs-all protein alignment", "Steinegger & Söding, Nat Biotechnol 2017",
  "ORFannotate", "ORF calling, protein/UTR sequences, NMD prediction", "---",
  "pigeon", "Structural classification and artifact removal", "SQANTI3 lineage",
  "DuckDB", "Columnar store for the ENDome tables and the pair enumeration", "Raasveldt & Mühleisen, SIGMOD 2019",
  "Gower's coefficient", "Combination of mixed-type, incomplete features", "Gower, Biometrics 1971",
  "Bit-score ratio", "Length-independent normalisation of alignment scores", "Rasko et al., BMC Bioinformatics 2005",
```

# ENDome Overview {.spacer #overview}

This section puts the `r length(endomes)` ENDomes of **`r wc$prefix`** side by side. 

## ENDome numbers

Here, we describe the merging of transcripts into bins.

+ `Singleton bins`: share of the bins with a single member transcript, which score 1 by construction.
+ `Transcripts merged`: share of the binned transcripts that are not the representative of their bin, whether merged by overlap or by proximity (see [Transcript Accounting](#transcript-accounting)).
+ `Genes with 2+ bins`: share of the genes with at least one bin that carry two or more. These are the genes where a usage shift can be tested downstream.

```{r overview1-table, echo=FALSE}
overview1_tbl <- endome_info %>%
  asEndome() %>%
  dplyr::select(endome, orf_filter_label, txEnd_label, width_label) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(tx_summary, by = "endome") %>%
  dplyr::left_join(bin_summary, by = "endome") %>%
  dplyr::left_join(
    gene_bins_df %>%
      dplyr::group_by(endome) %>%
      dplyr::summarise(pct_genes_multi = mean(n_bins >= 2), .groups = "drop"),
    by = "endome")

overview1_tbl %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    `ORF filter` = orf_filter_label, Site = txEnd_label, Width = width_label,
    Transcripts = fmtInt(n_transcripts),
    Bins = fmtInt(n_bins),
    `Singleton bins` = fmtPct(n_singleton / n_bins),
    `Transcripts merged` = fmtPct((n_members - n_bins) / n_members),
    `Not binned` = fmtPct(n_unbinned / n_transcripts),
    `Genes with 2+ bins` = fmtPct(pct_genes_multi)
  ) %>%
  renderTable(style = "md", align = c("l", "l", "l", rep("r", 6)),
              caption = sprintf("ENDome numbers of %s.", wc$prefix)) %>%
  kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 3, "Transcripts and bins" = 6)) %>%
  kableExtra::collapse_rows(columns = 1, valign = "top")
```

Note that ENDomes that differ only in their width are expected to have the same bin ratios and scores. The width sets the length of the truncated window, but which transcripts are merged together is decided by `merge_distance` (`r merge_distance` bp here), so every width produces the same bins. Only how their members are counted changes, as merged by overlap or by proximity (see [Transcript Accounting](#transcript-accounting)).

## Information content by ENDome {.tabset .break3}

The normalized score of the bins with at least two transcripts:

### Normalized Information Score {-}

```{r overview-bands_1, fig.height = overview_fig_height, fig.width = 10}
#' Score bands of the merged bins of every ENDome, one panel per ORF filter
#'
#' @param score_col Score variant, a column of merged_bins
#' @param title Title of the figure
plotBandsByEndome <- function(score_col, title){
  band_by_endome <- merged_bins %>%
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(.data[[score_col]])) %>%
    dplyr::count(endome, band = scoreBand(.data[[score_col]])) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(endome) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(prop = n / sum(n)) %>%
    dplyr::ungroup() %>%
    dplyr::left_join(asEndome(dplyr::select(endome_info, endome, orf_filter_label, short_label)),
                     by = "endome") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      short_label = factor(short_label, levels = unique(endome_info$short_label)),
      orf_filter_label = factor(orf_filter_label, levels = unique(endome_info$orf_filter_label))
    )

  ## Panel heights proportional to the ENDomes of each ORF filter
  filter_n_endomes <- as.numeric(table(endome_info$orf_filter_label)[levels(band_by_endome$orf_filter_label)])

  band_by_endome %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = prop, y = forcats::fct_rev(short_label), fill = band)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.75, colour = "grey25", linewidth = 0.25) +
    geom_text(aes(label = ifelse(prop >= 0.04, fmtPct(prop, 0.1), "")),
              position = position_stack(vjust = 0.5), size = 3.2) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = band_palette, drop = FALSE) +
    scale_x_continuous(labels = scales::percent, expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0))) +
    ggh4x::facet_wrap2(ggplot2::vars(orf_filter_label), ncol = 1, scales = "free_y") +
    ggh4x::force_panelsizes(rows = filter_n_endomes) +
    guides(fill = guide_legend(reverse = TRUE)) +
    labs(
      x = "Proportion of merged bins", y = NULL, fill = "Score band",
      title = title,
      subtitle = sprintf("%s | bins with two or more member transcripts", wc$prefix)
    ) +
    theme_endome(legend_pos = "right", base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid.major.y = element_blank())
}

plotBandsByEndome("info_score_norm", "Normalized information content by ENDome")
```

# Transcript Accounting {.spacer #transcript-accounting}

Before looking at the score distributions, this section showcases how the transcripts and bins of each ENDome are counted. For each ENDome, we generate the following tables:

+ The first describes the **input transcriptome**, what `txendcutr` was handed after the ORF filter. It is the same for every ENDome of an ORF filter.
+ The second describes the **ENDome** it produced, how many quantification units exist and how many of them are genuine merges.
+ The third describes **how each transcript ended up in its bin**. A transcript either is the representative of its bin, was merged because its truncated region is identical to another transcript of the same gene (*merged by overlap*), or was folded in because its truncation site fell within `merge_distance` of the representative's (*merged by proximity*).

Note that `txendcutr` drops a transcript before binning when its truncated exon structure is identical to another transcript's of the same gene. After truncating both to the window of the ENDome, the two are literally the same sequence and no assay could tell them apart. They are kept in the database so they remain traceable, attached to the bin of the transcript that superseded them, and counted in `n_members`. This is the conservative choice, as `n_members` then reports how many annotated transcripts the bin speaks for, rather than how many distinct truncated sequences went into it.

## Transcripts and bins {`r tab_class`}

```{r accounting, results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
renderTabsetByEndome(function(e){
  tx <- forEndome(tx_summary, e)
  b <- forEndome(bin_summary, e)  
  n_proximity <- tx$n_transcripts - tx$n_unbinned - tx$n_superseded - b$n_bins

  tibble::tribble(
    ~Quantity, ~N, ~Denominator, ~Definition,
    # Transcriptome
    "Transcripts", tx$n_transcripts, NA_real_, "ORF-filtered transcriptome; the input to txendcutr",
    "Genes", tx$n_genes, NA_real_, "Distinct gene_id across those transcripts",
    "Transcripts with a called ORF", tx$n_with_orf, tx$n_transcripts, "aa_id is not missing (ORFannotate)",
    "Transcripts predicted NMD-sensitive", tx$n_nmd, tx$n_transcripts, "50-nt rule applied by ORFannotate",
    # Bins
    "Bins in the ENDome", b$n_bins, NA_real_, "The quantification units after truncation; one representative transcript each",
    "Singleton bins", b$n_singleton, b$n_bins, "One member transcript; score 1 by construction, excluded from every summary below",
    "Multi-transcript bins", b$n_multi, b$n_bins, "Two or more member transcripts; the bins that can lose information",
    # Transcripts in bins
    "Representative transcripts", b$n_bins, tx$n_transcripts, "Transcripts that are representative of their bin",
    "Transcripts merged by overlap", tx$n_superseded, tx$n_transcripts, "Transcripts merged because they overlap exactly after truncation",
    "Transcripts merged by proximity", n_proximity, tx$n_transcripts, "Transcripts merged because they fell within merge_distance of the representative",
    "Transcripts not binned", tx$n_unbinned, tx$n_transcripts, "Dropped by the truncation, e.g. no 3' UTR in a UTR ENDome"
  ) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      N = as.numeric(N),
      `%` = dplyr::if_else(is.na(Denominator), "", paste0(fmtNum(100 * N / Denominator, 1), "%")),
      .after = N
    ) %>%
    dplyr::select(-Denominator) %>%
    renderTable(style = "md", align = c("l", "r", "r", "l"),
                caption = sprintf("Transcript and bin information of %s.", endome_labels[[e]])) %>%
    kableExtra::pack_rows("Input transcriptome", 1, 4, label_row_css = "background-color: #CCC; color: #fff;") %>%
    kableExtra::pack_rows("ENDome properties", 5, 7, label_row_css = "background-color: #CCC; color: #fff;") %>%
    kableExtra::pack_rows("Bin composition", 8, 11, label_row_css = "background-color: #CCC; color: #fff;") %>%
    kableExtra::column_spec(1, bold = TRUE, width = "28%") %>%
    kableExtra::column_spec(2:3, width = "8%") %>%
    kableExtra::column_spec(4, width = "56%", color = "#555")
})
```

## Reference isoforms {`r filter_tab_class`}

Transcripts are split below by the reference isoform flag (see [Methods](#methods)). 

```{r ref-isoform-table, results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
renderTabsetByFilter(function(f){
  ## Every ENDome of an ORF filter has the same transcripts, so the first one is used
  e <- endome_info$endome[endome_info$orf_filter == f][1]

  ref_isoform_tbl <- ref_isoform_counts %>%
    forEndome(e) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      group = dplyr::if_else(ref_isoform %in% TRUE, "Reference isoforms", "Other transcripts"),
      Class = dplyr::if_else(ref_isoform %in% TRUE, subcategory, structural_category)
    ) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(group, Class) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(N = sum(n), .groups = "drop") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(
      `%` = paste0(fmtNum(100 * N / sum(N), 1), "%"),
      group = factor(group, levels = c("Reference isoforms", "Other transcripts"))
    ) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(group, dplyr::desc(N))

  n_ref_rows <- sum(ref_isoform_tbl$group == "Reference isoforms")

  ref_isoform_kbl <- ref_isoform_tbl %>%
    dplyr::select(Class, N, `%`) %>%
    renderTable(style = "md", align = c("l", "r", "r"),
                caption = sprintf("Transcripts of the %s ORF filter by reference isoform status.", filter_tab_labels[[f]]))
  if(n_ref_rows > 0){
    ref_isoform_kbl <- ref_isoform_kbl %>%
      kableExtra::pack_rows("Reference isoforms (ref_isoform)", 1, n_ref_rows,
                            label_row_css = "background-color: #CCC; color: #fff;")
  }
  if(n_ref_rows < nrow(ref_isoform_tbl)){
    ref_isoform_kbl <- ref_isoform_kbl %>%
      kableExtra::pack_rows("Other transcripts", n_ref_rows + 1, nrow(ref_isoform_tbl),
                            label_row_css = "background-color: #CCC; color: #fff;")
  }
  ref_isoform_kbl
})
```

# Bin Size Distribution {.spacer}

The size of a bin is the number of transcripts it stands for, and it is the most direct measure of how much merging took place. A singleton bin keeps its transcript resolved and scores 1 by construction. This section shows both the number of bins and the number of transcripts contained in different bin sizes.

```{r bin-size-data}
## Bins and transcripts per bin size
bin_size_table <- bin_information %>%
  dplyr::count(endome, n_members, name = "n_bins") %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(n_members, .by_group = TRUE) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    n_transcripts = n_members * n_bins,
    pct_bins = n_bins / sum(n_bins),
    pct_transcripts = n_transcripts / sum(n_transcripts),
    cum_pct_bins = cumsum(pct_bins),
    cum_pct_transcripts = cumsum(pct_transcripts)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup()

## One class per bin size up to 14, and the rest pooled into "15+"
bin_size_long <- bin_size_table %>%
  dplyr::mutate(size_class = sizeClass(n_members, breaks = 1:14)) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome, size_class) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across(c(pct_bins, pct_transcripts), sum),
                   dplyr::across(c(cum_pct_bins, cum_pct_transcripts), max),
                   .groups = "drop") %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(-c(endome, size_class), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "pct") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(quantity = dplyr::recode(
    quantity,
    pct_bins = "% of bins", pct_transcripts = "% of transcripts",
    cum_pct_bins = "Cumulative % of bins",
    cum_pct_transcripts = "Cumulative % of transcripts"))

## Shares for both figures, and cumulative shares for the second
bin_size_shares <- dplyr::filter(bin_size_long, quantity %in% c("% of bins", "% of transcripts"))
bin_size_cumulative <- dplyr::filter(bin_size_long, grepl("^Cumulative", quantity))
```

## Bins by size {`r filter_tab_class`}

Each row gives the number of bins of one size (`Bins`), and the share of the ENDome's bins and of its transcripts they account for (`% bins`, `% transcripts`). Sizes above 12 are pooled into a single `13+` row.

```{r bin-size-table, results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
size_cols <- c(n_bins = "Bins", pct_bins = "% bins", pct_transcripts = "% transcripts")

renderTabsetByFilter(function(f){
  filter_endomes <- endome_info$endome[endome_info$orf_filter == f]
  wide_cols <- as.vector(t(outer(filter_endomes, names(size_cols), paste, sep = "__")))

  ## One row per size up to 12 and one group of columns per ENDome. Missing sizes have 0 bins
  size_wide <- bin_size_table %>%
    dplyr::filter(endome %in% filter_endomes) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(size = sizeClass(n_members, breaks = 1:12)) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(endome, size) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(dplyr::across(c(n_bins, pct_bins, pct_transcripts), sum), .groups = "drop") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(n_bins = fmtInt(n_bins), dplyr::across(c(pct_bins, pct_transcripts), \(x) fmtPct(x, 0.01))) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_wider(
      id_cols = size, names_from = endome, values_from = dplyr::all_of(names(size_cols)),
      names_glue = "{endome}__{.value}",
      values_fill = list(n_bins = "0", pct_bins = fmtPct(0, 0.01), pct_transcripts = fmtPct(0, 0.01))
    ) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(size) %>%
    dplyr::select(size, dplyr::all_of(wide_cols)) %>%
    as.data.frame()

  ## The same three headers under every ENDome (a data.frame allows duplicated names)
  names(size_wide) <- c("Size", rep(unname(size_cols), length(filter_endomes)))
  endome_groups <- stats::setNames(rep(length(size_cols), length(filter_endomes)),
                                   endome_info$short_label[match(filter_endomes, endome_info$endome)])

  size_wide %>%
    renderTable(caption = sprintf("Bins of each size in the ENDomes of the %s ORF filter, and the share of the bins and of the transcripts of each ENDome they account for.",
                                  filter_tab_labels[[f]]),
                style = "md", align = c("l", rep("r", ncol(size_wide) - 1)), row_padding = "3px") %>%
    kableExtra::add_header_above(c(" " = 1, endome_groups))
})
```

## Cumulative distribution {`r tab_class`}

The bars of the previous figure, with their cumulative curves overlaid. Each curve gives the share of bins (or transcripts) in bins of at most that size. The transcript curve always lies below the bin curve, and the wider the gap between them, the more the transcriptome is concentrated in a few large bins.

```{r bin-size-cumulative-plot, results = "asis", echo = FALSE, fig.height = 5, fig.width = 12}
renderTabsetByEndome(function(e){
  ggplot(mapping = aes(x = size_class, y = pct)) +
    geom_col(data = forEndome(bin_size_shares, e), aes(fill = quantity),
             position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.8, colour = "black", linewidth = 0.4) +
    geom_line(data = forEndome(bin_size_cumulative, e), aes(colour = quantity, group = quantity),

      subtitle = endomeSubtitle(e)) +

           colour = guide_legend(order = 2)) +
    theme_endome(base_size = 13, legend_pos = "right")
})
```

## Bins per gene {`r tab_class`}

The number of bins of a gene decides what the downstream analysis can test for it. Differential UTR/transcript usage asks how a gene's counts are split across its bins, so a gene with a single bin has nothing to test, even if its overall expression changes.

Genes with two or more bins are therefore the population every usage result is conditioned on. They are also the genes where the information content of each bin matters most, since a usage shift between two bins is only interpretable if each bin stands for something coherent.

```{r bins-per-gene-plot, results = "asis", echo = FALSE, fig.height = 4.5}
renderTabsetByEndome(function(e){
  genes <- forEndome(gene_bins_df, e)

  genes %>%
    dplyr::mutate(bins_class = sizeClass(n_bins, breaks = 1:9)) %>%
    dplyr::count(bins_class) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(pct = n/sum(n)) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = bins_class, y = pct)) +
    geom_col(fill = col_bars, width = 0.7, color = "black", linewidth = 0.5) +
    geom_text(aes(label = fmtPct(pct, 0.1)), vjust = -0.4, size = 3, colour = "black") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::percent_format(accuracy = 1), expand = c(0, 0, 0.12, 0)) +
    scale_x_discrete() +
    labs(
      x = "Bins per gene", y = "% of genes",
      title = "Distribution of bins per gene",
      subtitle = sprintf("%s | %s genes carry at least one bin", endome_labels[[e]], fmtInt(nrow(genes)))
    ) +
    theme_endome(base_size = 11)
})
```

# Information Content {.spacer #information-content}

This section describes the information scores of the merged bins (two or more member transcripts) of every ENDome, under the three score variants described in the [Methods](#methods). Singleton bins score 1 by construction and are left out (see [Singletons](#singletons)), except in the `All bins` rows of the summary table.

## Distribution of information scores {`r tab_class`}

The figure below shows the distribution of each score variant over the merged bins. The box carries the median and the quartiles, and the diamond the mean. The violins are cut at the lowest and highest score of each variant, and use a narrow bandwidth so that their shape stays close to the underlying counts

```{r score-summary-data}
score_tbl <- dplyr::bind_rows(
  summariseScores(scores_long, endome, score) %>% dplyr::mutate(subset = "All bins", .after = score),
  summariseScores(merged_long, endome, score) %>% dplyr::mutate(subset = "Merged bins (n >= 2)", .after = score)
) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(endome, score) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(dplyr::across(dplyr::starts_with("pct_"), \(x) fmtPct(x, 0.1)))
```

```{r score-distribution, results = "asis", echo = FALSE, fig.height = 5.5, fig.width = 10}
binwidth <- 0.01

renderTabsetByEndome(function(e){
```

The same scores grouped into bands, which makes the share of the bins at each level of concordance easier to compare between the score variants.

## Distribution by bin size {`r tab_class`}

The figure below shows the density of each score variant within each bin size as a ridge, with one class per size. A ridge sitting close to 1 means that the merges of that size preserve everything the features can see, while a ridge that spreads leftwards as the size grows means that concordance degrades with bin size. Below the figure of each ENDome, its summary table by bin size can be expanded.

```{r score-by-size-data}
score_by_size_tbl <- merged_long %>%
  summariseScores(endome, score, size_class) %>%
  dplyr::filter(n_bins > 0) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(endome, score, size_class) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(pct_below_09 = fmtPct(pct_below_09, 0.1))
```

