## Median by bin size {`r tab_class`}

Collapsing each size to a single number makes the trend across sizes easier to follow, at the cost of hiding the shape of each distribution. 
<!-- The ribbons are the 95% confidence intervals of the median. They describe how precisely the median of each size is estimated, not the spread of the individual bins. -->

```{r score-median-by-size, results = "asis", echo = FALSE, fig.height = 5}
#' One end of the 95% CI of the median, from the order statistics of x
#'
#' The ranks of the two ends come from a Binomial(n, 0.5). Below 6 values the CI is the whole range
medianCI <- function(x, side = c("lower", "upper"), level = 0.95){
  side <- match.arg(side)
  x <- sort(x[!is.na(x)])
  n <- length(x)
  if(n == 0) return(NA_real_)
  lower_rank <- max(1, stats::qbinom((1 - level) / 2, n, 0.5))
  if(side == "lower") x[lower_rank] else x[n - lower_rank + 1]
}

score_median_by_size <- merged_long %>%
  dplyr::filter(n_members <= max_size_median) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome, score, n_members) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_bins = dplyr::n(),
    median = stats::median(value, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_lo = medianCI(value, "lower"),
    median_hi = medianCI(value, "upper"),
    .groups = "drop"
  )

renderTabsetByEndome(function(e){
  forEndome(score_median_by_size, e) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = n_members, y = median, color = score, fill = score)) +
    # geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = median_lo, ymax = median_hi), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(size = 1.6) +
    scale_colour_manual(values = score_palette) +
    scale_fill_manual(values = score_palette, guide = "none") +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = seq(2, max_size_median, 2), expand = c(0, 0.5, 0, 0.5)) +
    labs(
      x = "Bin size", y = "Median information content", colour = NULL,
      title = "Median information content as a function of bin size",
      # subtitle = sprintf("%s | Ribbons are 95%% confidence intervals of the median", endome_labels[[e]])
      subtitle = endome_labels[[e]]
    ) +
    theme_endome(legend_pos = "top", base_size = 13)
})
```

## Effect of dropping the reference-state agreements {`r tab_class`}

The asymmetric variant differs from the default one in that a component where both members sit in the reference state is treated as non-comparable rather than as an agreement. The histogram below is the per-bin difference `info_score_asymmetric - info_score_norm`, which helps identify exactly how much of the default score depends on these kinds of agreements. A bin at a negative value is one that looked more concordant than it is. Once the "both canonical, both non-NMD" agreements are removed, the weight they carried shifts onto the protein and CDS length components.

```{r score-delta-asym, results = "asis", echo = FALSE, fig.height = 5}
renderTabsetByEndome(level = 3, function(e){
  forEndome(merged_bins, e) %>%
    dplyr::mutate(delta = info_score_asymmetric - info_score_norm) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = delta)) +
    geom_histogram(bins = 60, fill = col_delta, color = "black") +
    geom_vline(xintercept = 0, linetype = "dashed", colour = "grey40") +
    scale_y_continuous(labels = scales::comma, expand = c(0, 0, 0.1, 0)) +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = 0) +
    labs(
      x = "info_score_asymmetric - info_score_norm", y = "Number of bins",
      title = "Effect of dropping the reference-state agreements",
      subtitle = endome_labels[[e]]
    ) +
    theme_endome(base_size = 13)
})
```

# Component contribution to Information Content {.spacer}

The `bin_information` table stores the weighted mean dissimilarity of each component over the comparable pairs of that bin. Two separate questions follow from it: **what each component does to the score**, and **how often each component can be measured at all**. The first is a matter of disagreement and weight, the second of missing evidence.

```{r component-data}
component_long <- merged_bins %>%
  dplyr::select(endome, bin_id, n_members, size_class, dplyr::starts_with("mean_d_")) %>%
  tidyr::pivot_longer(dplyr::starts_with("mean_d_"), names_to = "component", values_to = "mean_d") %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    component = stringr::str_remove(component, "^mean_d_"),
    weight = component_weights[component]
  )

component_summary <- component_long %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome, component, weight) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    pct_comparable = mean(!is.na(mean_d)),
    pct_bins_perfect = mean(mean_d <= 1e-9, na.rm = TRUE),
    median_d = stats::median(mean_d, na.rm = TRUE),
    mean_d = mean(mean_d, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    weighted_d = weight * mean_d,
    contribution = weighted_d / sum(weighted_d, na.rm = TRUE)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::ungroup() %>%
  dplyr::relocate(endome, component, weight, pct_comparable, mean_d, median_d, pct_bins_perfect) %>%
  dplyr::arrange(endome, dplyr::desc(contribution))
```

## Effect of each component 

It is important to distinguish between how dissimilar members are on a given component, and how much that component actually affects the final score. A component can be highly variable and still barely matter if its weight is small, and a heavily weighted component contributes nothing if its members always agree.

### Mean dissimilarity and weighted contribution {.unlisted .unnumbered .hidden-heading `r tab_class` }

+ **Mean dissimilarity**: average of `mean_d_<components>` across every merged bin where the component is comparable. Each bin contributes its own weighted mean over its comparable pairs, and bins where the component is `NA` are dropped rather than counted as 0. It is unaffected by the configured weights.
+ **Weighted contribution**: the same mean multiplied by the component's weight.

```{r component-plot, results = "asis", echo = FALSE, fig.height = 5}
renderTabsetByEndome(level = 4, function(e){
  forEndome(component_summary, e) %>%
    dplyr::select(component, weight, mean_d, weighted_d) %>%
    tidyr::pivot_longer(c(mean_d, weighted_d), names_to = "quantity", values_to = "value") %>%
    dplyr::mutate(quantity = dplyr::recode(quantity, mean_d = "Mean dissimilarity", weighted_d = "Weighted contribution")) %>%
    ggplot(aes(y = reorder(component, value), x = value, fill = weight)) +
    geom_col(width = 0.65, color = "black") +
    scale_fill_viridis_c(begin = 0.25, end = 0.9, name = "Weight") +
    scale_x_continuous(expand = c(0, 0, 0.1, 0)) +
    facet_wrap(~ quantity, scales = "free_x") +
    guides(fill = guide_colorbar(
      barheight = unit(45, "mm"), barwidth = unit(6, "mm"),
      frame.colour = "black",
      theme = theme(legend.ticks = element_line(linewidth = 0.6, color = "black"))
    )) +
    labs(
      x = NULL, y = NULL,
      title = "What drives the Information Score",
      subtitle = endome_labels[[e]]
    ) +
    theme_endome(base_size = 13, legend_pos = "right") +
    theme(
      legend.title = element_text(margin = margin(b = 10)),
      panel.spacing.x = unit(1, "lines")
    )
})
```

### Component dissimilarity by bin size {`r tab_class`}

Following these results, we can split the same means by bin size to observe where the degradation comes from as the number of transcripts merged grows. The aggregate above is dominated by the 2-member bins (bulk of the population), so a component that only misbehaves in large bins might be invisible. The shape of each line shows how each component behaves across bin sizes. A flat line means that the component is equally concordant whatever the size, while a positive slope represents a component whose dissimilarity increases as more transcripts are folded together.

```{r component-by-size, results = "asis", echo = FALSE, fig.height = 5}
component_mean_by_size <- component_long %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(mean_d), !is.na(size_class)) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome, component, size_class) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    mean = mean(mean_d, na.rm = TRUE),
    se = stats::sd(mean_d, na.rm = TRUE) / sqrt(dplyr::n()),
    .groups = "drop")

renderTabsetByEndome(level = 4, function(e){
  forEndome(component_mean_by_size, e) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = size_class, y = mean, group = component, fill = component, color = component)) +
    geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = mean - 1.96*se, ymax = mean + 1.96*se), alpha = 0.2, color = NA) +
    geom_line(linewidth = 0.9) +
    geom_point(size = 1.8) +
    scale_x_discrete(expand = c(0, 0.2, 0, 0.2)) +
    scale_fill_viridis_d(option = "turbo", begin = 0.1, end = 0.9) +
    scale_colour_viridis_d(option = "turbo", begin = 0.1, end = 0.9) +
    labs(
      x = "Bin size", y = "Mean dissimilarity", colour = "Component", fill = "Component",
      title = "Component dissimilarity across bin sizes",
      subtitle = endome_labels[[e]]
    ) +
    theme_endome(legend_pos = "right")
})
```

### Invariant components

A component can end up contributing little to the score for two very different reasons:

+ **Rarely comparable**: if a component cannot be compared between two transcripts, it does not score 0, it drops out of the Gower distance and its weight is redistributed onto the remaining components.

+ **Comparable but invariant**: a component whose dissimilarity is close to 0 in almost every bin where it is measured spends weight on agreement that was never in question. This is the main motivation for the *asymmetric* variant of the information score, which is designed to correct components having a distribution very heavily skewed towards their baseline.

The table below lists, for every ENDome, the components that are effectively invariant (identical in more than `r fmtPct(invariant_threshold, 1)` of the merged bins), and the share of the total weight that is being spent on agreement that was never in question.

```{r component-invariant, echo = FALSE}
component_summary %>%
  dplyr::mutate(invariant = !is.na(pct_bins_perfect) & pct_bins_perfect > invariant_threshold) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    components = paste(sprintf("<code>%s</code>", component[invariant]), collapse = ", "),
    weight_share = sum(weight[invariant], na.rm = TRUE) / sum(weight, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::left_join(asEndome(dplyr::select(endome_info, endome, label)), by = "endome") %>%
  dplyr::transmute(
    ENDome = label,
    `Invariant components` = dplyr::if_else(components == "", "None", components),
    `Share of the total weight` = fmtPct(weight_share)
  ) %>%
  renderTable(style = "md", escape = FALSE, align = c("l", "l", "r"),
              caption = "Components identical in almost every merged bin, and the share of the total weight they carry.")
```

## Component comparability {`r tab_class`}

Having seen what each component does when it can be measured, the remaining question is how often that is the case. A pair of transcripts that cannot be scored on any single component is not a concordant pair, it is an unknown one, and it is recorded as `NA` rather than as agreement.

Within each size class, `N. Pairs` is the total number of within-bin pairs enumerated across every bin of the class, `N. Scored` how many of them received a Gower distance and `N. Unscored` the remainder. The last column reports the *mass deficit*. Recall that the normalized score divides Rao's $Q$ by the comparable pair mass $M$, and that $M = 1 - 1/n$ when every pair of an $n$-member bin could be scored. The deficit is the gap $\left(1 - 1/n\right) - M$ (i.e. the weight carried by the pairs that could not be scored at all). For `info_score` (Rao's default approach), only the numerator loses them, so an unscored pair contributes 0 to $Q$, which is indistinguishable from a perfectly concordant pair. The non-normalised score therefore reads "unknown" as "identical" and is inflated by exactly the deficit.

```{r comparability-data}
comparability_tbl <- merged_bins %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    fully_scored = n_pairs_scored >= n_pairs,
    mass_deficit = pmax(0, (1 - 1 / n_members) - pair_mass)
  ) %>%
  dplyr::group_by(endome, size_class) %>%
  dplyr::summarise(
    n_bins = dplyr::n(),
    n_pairs = sum(n_pairs),
    n_scored = sum(n_pairs_scored),
    n_unscored = sum(n_pairs) - sum(n_pairs_scored),
    pct_pairs_scored = sum(n_pairs_scored) / sum(n_pairs),
    pct_bins_fully_scored = mean(fully_scored),
    max_mass_deficit = max(mass_deficit, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  ) %>%
  dplyr::mutate(
    dplyr::across(c(pct_pairs_scored, pct_bins_fully_scored), \(x) fmtPct(x, 0.1)),
    max_mass_deficit = dplyr::if_else(max_mass_deficit < 1e-9, "0", fmtNum(max_mass_deficit, 4))
  )
```

```{r comparability, results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
renderTabsetByEndome(function(e){
  forEndome(comparability_tbl, e) %>%
    dplyr::select(
      `Size Class` = size_class, `N. Bins` = n_bins, `N. Pairs` = n_pairs,
      `N. Scored` = n_scored, `N. Unscored` = n_unscored,
      `% Pairs Scored` = pct_pairs_scored,
      `% of Bins Fully Scored` = pct_bins_fully_scored,
      `Max Mass Deficit` = max_mass_deficit
    ) %>%
    renderTable(style = "md",
                caption = sprintf("Within-bin pairs of %s that could be scored on at least one component, counted per size class.",
                                  endome_labels[[e]]),
                align = c("l", rep("r", 7)))
})
```

# Bin analysis {.spacer}

## Least concordant bins {`r tab_class`}

The table ranks every merged bin by its normalized information score, and reports the `r n_worst_bins` lowest. Alongside the three score variants, it prints the per-component means, so the reason a given bin scores badly can be read off the row.

```{r worst-bins, results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
renderTabsetByEndome(function(e){
  forEndome(merged_bins, e) %>%
    dplyr::left_join(bin_gene_names, by = c("endome", "bin_id")) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(info_score_norm) %>%
    dplyr::select(bin_id, gene_name, n_members, n_superseded,
                  info_score_norm, info_score, info_score_asymmetric,
                  dplyr::starts_with("mean_d_")) %>%
    renderTable(style = "html", limit = n_worst_bins, pageLength = 10, digits = 2,
                caption = sprintf("The %s least concordant merged bins of %s, ranked by the normalized score.",
                                  n_worst_bins, endome_labels[[e]]))
})
```

## Least concordant large bins {`r tab_class`}

Most likely, the ranking above is dominated by small bins with two unrelated transcripts. The following table represents the same information but for bins with at least `r min_members_large` members, as these bins absorb many transcripts at once and a low score here removes more of the transcriptome from interpretation than any single small bin does.

```{r worst-bins-large, results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
renderTabsetByEndome(function(e){
  forEndome(merged_bins, e) %>%
    dplyr::left_join(bin_gene_names, by = c("endome", "bin_id")) %>%
    dplyr::filter(n_members >= min_members_large) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(info_score_norm) %>%
    dplyr::select(bin_id, gene_name, n_members, n_superseded,
                  info_score, info_score_norm, info_score_asymmetric, n_pairs, pair_mass) %>%
    renderTable(style = "html", limit = n_worst_bins, pageLength = 10, digits = 2,
                caption = sprintf("The %s most damaging merges of %s among the larger bins (%s+ members).",
                                  n_worst_bins, endome_labels[[e]], min_members_large))
})
```

## Specific genes {`r tab_class`}

A gene whose bins are all clean supports an interpretable result, even if one of them merged several transcripts, while a gene whose bins are all mixtures does not. The table below aggregates to the gene, keeping genes that carry at least `r min_merged_bins_gene` merged bins (the ones where the usage test has something to compare), and ranking them by the mean normalized score across those bins. Here, `min_score` is added because a gene can have a respectable mean and still contain one badly mixed bin, which is enough to make a shift involving that bin uninterpretable. These are the genes where a DTU call is less likely to have interpretable biological consequences.

```{r worst-genes, results = "asis", echo = FALSE}
renderTabsetByEndome(function(e){
  forEndome(merged_bins, e) %>%
    dplyr::filter(!is.na(gene_id)) %>%
    dplyr::group_by(gene_id) %>%
    dplyr::summarise(
      n_merged_bins = dplyr::n(),
      n_members = sum(n_members),
      min_score = min(info_score_norm, na.rm = TRUE),
      mean_score = mean(info_score_norm, na.rm = TRUE),
      .groups = "drop"
    ) %>%
    dplyr::filter(n_merged_bins >= min_merged_bins_gene) %>%
    dplyr::arrange(mean_score) %>%
    dplyr::left_join(gene_names, by = "gene_id") %>%
    dplyr::relocate(gene_name, .after = gene_id) %>%
    renderTable(style = "html", limit = n_worst_bins, pageLength = 10, digits = 2,
                caption = sprintf("Genes of %s with at least %s merged bins and the lowest mean information content.",
                                  endome_labels[[e]], min_merged_bins_gene))
})
```

<!-- # Future work {.spacer} -->

<!-- The Bin Information Content is still work in development. Every component and their weights is still provisional. The score is best read as an ordering of bins, rather than as a calibrated quantity. Points below are the future modifications or things to consider when using this metric: -->

<!-- + **Scoring weights are not stored in the database**: from the DuckDB alone, the component weights are not accessible. In the future, they should have their own table. -->
<!-- + **Uniform member weights**: every member of a bin contributes $p_i = 1/n$ to Rao's quadratic entropy. Weighting members by expression is the natural fix and is what the $p_i$ in the formula is there for, but abundances do not exist at this point of the pipeline. Possible implementations at this point involves ideas such as the transcript support level, the SQANTI3 structural category (down-weighting novel or single-exon models against full splice matches), or  whether the transcript is in the reference annotation. -->
<!-- + **Protein similarity is alignment-level, not domain-level**: the bit-score ratio says how much of a protein is shared, not exactly which part. Two isoform different by a functional domain can score high. Pfam/InterPro annotation is the next logical step. -->
<!-- + **Weights are manually decided**: the current values are subject to change and are biased towards the specifics of each analysis. Any absolute threshold drawn on the score inherits that bias. -->
<!-- + **Information contained in the ORF sequence itself are not accounted for**: stability measurements such as AREs or mRNA binding sites are not scored at this stage, and a bin can be perfectly concordant in their ORF characteristics but different in their regulatory contexts. -->
